source.title: (Mis)Fitting: A Survey of Scaling Laws
source.authors: Margaret Li; Sneha Kudugunta; Luke S. Zettlemoyer

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The paper refits scaling laws under different data, training, parameter-counting, checkpoint-selection, and fitting choices. It reports that these choices can materially change predicted compute-optimal allocations, directly qualifying the stability of those allocations and documenting fit-dependence.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the authors’ own refits and sensitivity analyses. Survey summaries and findings attributed to prior works are not recorded as this paper’s results. The paper does not report a systematic test of whether larger-run held-out losses depart from laws fit on smaller runs.
record.test_reason: §7 refits compute-optimal laws on three loss datasets: reconstructed Chinchilla, Porian et al., and the authors' own 12M–1B models. It varies law form, learning rate, scale and D/N coverage, N/C counting, checkpoint use, initialization, objective and optimizer, and shows the predicted N_opt/D_opt shift with these choices. That bears directly on V7 and on the stability claimed in V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that every fitting and setup decision they explored affects the final power-law fit, demonstrating the process's fragility. They call for thorough reporting (a checklist) and avoid prescriptive recommendations, since no known procedure guarantees a good fit.
record.recipe_differences: The paper refits existing training-loss data and its own language-model runs using related power-law forms, while varying fitting and setup decisions; it is not an end-to-end replication of either original study’s full training procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted allocations vary with power-law form, learning rate, scale and D/N coverage, embedding parameter counting, checkpoint selection, initialization, fitting objective, optimizer, and dataset.
record.problems: The paper reports most allocation-curve comparisons qualitatively rather than as tabulated fitted coefficients. The reconstructed Chinchilla data were extracted from a vector-based figure and the authors note a risk of extraction errors. Their own models range from 12 million to 1 billion parameters; the paper does not validate small-run loss extrapolations against newly trained much larger runs. The paper’s checklist notes that the authors do not evaluate correctness beyond comparison with literature.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Prior-work survey findings and reported results from other papers are not included as this paper’s experimental results.

untested.parts: No test of whether held-out loss follows a power law over orders of magnitude; the paper fits allocation curves only.
Extrapolated allocations are not validated against larger runs. The authors state they do not evaluate correctness beyond comparison with the literature.
No independent determination of the true compute-optimal N/D (e.g. large IsoFLOP sweeps). The paper does not decide between the Kaplan and Hoffmann exponents.
No fixed-N depth or width variation.
Other modalities and regimes appear only in the survey, not in the paper's own experiments.
Data source and learning-rate schedule are not varied as controlled factors. The three datasets differ in many ways at once.

missing.what: Using all mid-training checkpoints makes fits more consistent when other fitting choices are varied. Appendix E repeats all analyses with all checkpoints.
Appendix D: sweeping the learning rate gives a less stable fit than fixing it.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The reconstructed Chinchilla data derive from Hoffmann et al., but the refits are this paper's own. Most results are qualitative descriptions of plotted curves, with extrapolated N/D annotations at reference compute budgets; no exponents are tabulated. The study shows dependence of the fitted allocation, not of the true optimum. It therefore bears on V3 only by showing that published allocations rest on fragile fits.

versions.untested_parts: The paper fits loss-based laws but does not test whether held-out loss follows the claimed power laws across parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
It compares extrapolated allocation curves but does not validate small-run loss predictions against much larger runs.

It studies how fitting and setup choices change predicted optimal parameter and data allocations. It does not establish a single stable exponent for parameter count or token count versus compute, nor directly compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann growth-rate claims as invariant empirical laws.
No controlled test of depth, width, or architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
The survey discusses other modalities and training regimes, but the paper’s own sensitivity experiments do not test whether the same power-law form holds across them.
It does not test downstream task performance scaling or its prediction from pretraining loss.
The experiments assess dependence on several fitting and training choices, but do not systematically vary every listed factor, such as data source or all training schedules.

rows.subject: Reconstructed Chinchilla data (Besiroglu et al. (2024))
rows.size_stated: 245 datapoints from final checkpoints; underlying run sizes not stated here
rows.operation_detail: Refit the Hoffmann form with and without the constraint α = β

conditions.value: reconstructed Chinchilla data
final checkpoints

rows.measure: Fitted compute-optimal parameter and data allocation
rows.baseline: Hoffmann form without α = β; comparison reference is the reported Hoffmann et al. (2022) law
rows.value: Constraining α = β yields a law much closer to the reported Hoffmann law; initializing from reported Hoffmann coefficients also yields a nearly identical fit (the latter comparison is reported separately in R16).
rows.note: The paper describes the fitted allocation curves qualitatively; no numerical exponents for these refits are given.
rows.check: For V7 the fit-dependence is observed: constraining α=β moves the fit toward Hoffmann. For V3 this is instability, not stability. The α=β constraint imposes equal N/D growth, so it is not independent evidence for Hoffmann's split. The R16 cross-reference in the value is about initialization, which is actually R10.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. V3: partial; alternative fitting constraints change the inferred allocation. Agreement after imposing α = β is not independent evidence for equal growth.
source_check.problem: The shared observed state fits V7 but overstates support for V3.

rows.subject: Authors’ Transformer LMs (12 million to 1 billion parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Refit the Hoffmann form with and without the constraint α = β

conditions.value: authors’ models
final checkpoints

rows.measure: Fitted compute-optimal parameter and data allocation
rows.baseline: Hoffmann form without α = β; comparison reference is the reported Hoffmann et al. (2022) law
rows.value: With α = β, the fit approaches the law reported by Hoffmann et al. (2022); the unconstrained form does not do so for this dataset. The Kaplan et al. (2020) form consistently implies an optimal data count of 1.
rows.note: The stated optimal data count of 1 is the authors’ reported outcome of fitting the Kaplan form, not a measured training-data optimum.
rows.check: V7 effect observed. The unconstrained form diverges from Hoffmann, and the Kaplan form degenerates to an optimal D of 1. Per §7.1 that degenerate Kaplan result holds across datasets and settings, not only the authors' models.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. V3: partial; the inferred allocation depends on the form. The Kaplan-form fit repeatedly predicts an optimal data count of 1; this is a fitting outcome, not a measured optimum.
source_check.problem: Observed fits V7, but not unqualified V3 stability; the Kaplan-form failure is not restricted to the authors' dataset.

rows.subject: Authors’ Transformer LMs (12 million to 1 billion parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Compare fitted laws using a learning-rate sweep, fixed learning rates, and all learning rates together

conditions.value: sweep at each (N, D) pair; alternatives are fixed 1e-3, fixed 2e-3, fixed 4e-3, or all learning rates
authors’ models

rows.measure: Fitted compute-optimal allocation curves and fitting loss
rows.baseline: Learning-rate sweep at each (N, D) pair
rows.value: Results vary dramatically. Using all learning rates gives a very similar law to sweeping; fixed 1e-3 gives the lowest optimization loss; fixed 4e-3 gives the closest match to the reported Hoffmann laws.
rows.note: The paper reports these comparisons in words; the plotted curves do not provide tabulated fitted coefficients.
rows.check: Text says results 'vary dramatically' across learning-rate settings, which is the V7 effect in full. Partial understates it.

source_check.correct: V7: observed. V3: partial. All-learning-rate and swept-learning-rate fits are similar; fixed 1e-3 gives the lowest fitting loss, and fixed 4e-3 gives the closest Hoffmann match.
source_check.problem: A shared observed state obscures the qualification of V3 by learning-rate choices.

rows.subject: Reconstructed Chinchilla data (Besiroglu et al. (2024)); Porian et al. (2024) training-loss data; authors’ Transformer LMs
rows.size_stated: Datasets include 245 reconstructed Chinchilla datapoints; Porian models range from 5 to 901 million parameters; authors’ models range from 12 million to 1 billion parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit on subsets restricted by model size or data-to-parameter ratio

conditions.value: all models; N up to about 100 million; N up to 400 million; D/N ≤ 18; or D/N ≥ 22
above 1022 FLOPs for the reported ratio-cut behavior

rows.value: The minimum or maximum D/N ratio tested skews results: above 1022 FLOPs, the D/N ≤ 18 subset fits optimal ratios below 18, while the D/N ≥ 22 subset fits ratios above 22. Removing the authors’ largest models also creates a major shift in predicted optimal D/N.
rows.note: The text gives the qualitative shifts and the stated thresholds, but not numerical fitted ratios for each curve.
rows.check: The D/N-range filter drives the fitted optimum to lie inside the filtered range (<18 or >22 above 1e22 FLOPs). This is a strong V7 effect. The compute threshold is 10^22 FLOPs, mis-rendered as '1022'. Overlaps R15.

source_check.correct: The compute threshold is 10^22 FLOPs, not 1022 FLOPs. Above it, fits restricted to D/N ≤ 18 and D/N ≥ 22 predict D/N < 18 and D/N > 22, respectively. V7: observed; V3: partial.
source_check.problem: The exponent is flattened in the threshold, and observed applies to sensitivity rather than unqualified allocation stability.

rows.subject: Authors’ Transformer LMs (12 million to 1 billion parameters)
